subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO FORMER PARLIAMENTARIAN, GERALD BALDWIN- MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I believe I have unanimous consent for this motion. Whereas the House of Commons just yesterday passed the freedom of information bill, and whereas my predecessor, Mr. Gerald Baldwin, worked tirelessly toward and supported the principle of freedom of information, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. All-mand) and the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That this House unanimously commend Gerald Baldwin for his unceasing work for freedom of information legislation, and further, for his years of dedicated service to his fellow countrymen.

subsubtopic: DEMAND FOR ASSISTANCE TO INDUSTRY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Last night the finance minister announced a special farm financial assistance program which provides for $200,000,000 over the next two years to assist farmers in financial distress. Naturally, we welcome such an announcement, but at the same time we fail to understand why similar assistance was not provided for the fishing industry which employs 80,000 Canadians and forms the backbone of the economy of the Atlantic provinces. Many companies have been forced into bankruptcy and the industry still faces an uncertain future. I would therefore
move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser):
That this House direct the Minister of Finance to provide immediate assistance to the fishing industry in a program similar to that which is now being offered to the agricultural industry.

That this House calls on the Minister of Agriculture to resign because of his unwillingness to deal with the number one problem for farmers in Canada-high interest rates.

speechtext:
Last night the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) said that "the private sector and the provinces could not be expected to accept income restraints unless the Government of Canada showed leadership in the conduct of its own affairs." During the past few days, the national press has reported that the assistant secretary to the cabinet for economic development policy, who receives a salary of approximately $75,000 a year, is to be sent to the south of

June 29, 1982
France for bilingual language training. This four-month joyride will cost Canadian taxpayers, whom the minister has asked to show restraint, some $11,800. While many Canadians and, I dare say, many hon. members opposite would be pleased to see one of the architects of the present budgetary fiascos deported, banished, or otherwise disposed of, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer):
That if this government is truly serious about showing leadership, and if it is serious about restraint, then the President of the Treasury Board should launch an immediate review of all such ridiculous and inexcusable examples of wasteful government spending.

subsubtopic: REDUCTION IN BUDGET-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the 1982-83 allocation in the 1980 budget for expenditures under the Western Development Fund was set at $750 million. Under the 1981 budget this allocation was cut by 75 per cent to $182 million. Under last night's budget the people of western Canada are further insulted, as the 1982-83 allocation receives a further massacre of 50 per cent. Now a further $92 million has gone from the pockets of westerners. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers):
That this House censure the Minister of Finance for his apparent lack of understanding in failing to appreciate the hopes and aspirations of westerners and his lack of honesty in failing to admit that this fund was a fraud from the date of its conception.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I, too, rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that the minister responsible for pensions has stated that the first priority of the Liberal government with regard to pension reform was to bring all senior citizens above the poverty line, and in view of the fact that single pensioners are still more
than $800 below the poverty line, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell):
That this House condemn the minister and the Liberal government for abandoning this commitment and instead cutting basic pension benefits by deindexation, which will require more and more pensioners to submit to a means test just to ensure that they fall no further below the poverty line than they are already, and that if the minister does not rescind last night's budgetary measure, she should resign.

subsubtopic: CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT POSITION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last night's budget once again ignored a matter of urgent necessity. Following "Consultation 81", the government made a public undertaking to act on the give-and-take tax proposals of the national voluntary organizations. Last week the Minister of State for Social Development (Mr. Chretien) told this House that he had personally raised this matter before the cabinet. Last night's budget, as well as November's discredited budget, demonstrated an abysmal ignorance of the potential caring contribution of Canada's voluntary sector during these times of social and economic hardship. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid):
That this House urge the government to admit to Canada's three million volunteers that it has no intention of encouraging a working partnership with the voluntary sector, and that its distrustful, interventionist grant policy was intended to undermine the time-proven ability of non-government agencies to deliver their sorely needed caring services.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR RESIGNATIONS OF PRIME MINISTER AND MINISTER OF FINANCE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, up until last night Canadians at least had hope. When Canadian workers asked for legitimate job creation, when Canadian businesses asked for tax reform to aid industrial recovery, when the Canadian economy demanded investment encouragement for plants, processes and opportunities, when
June 29, 1982

Canadian youth cried out for higher education and better training and when senior Canadians asked only for stable costs and a dignified retirement, this government gave them higher taxes, higher interest rates, higher debt, higher inflation, and higher unemployment. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker):
That the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister do the only worth-while remaining act of which they are capable, namely, resign before the downward economic spiral becomes a national economic disaster.

CALL FOR RESIGNATIONS OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in light of the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has forced public employees with low incomes to accept wage controls at the same percentage level as cabinet ministers and other senior bureaucrats and appointees earning over $100,000 a year, and since the Minister of Finance has encouraged other Canadians to accept this unjust system of sharing the economic burden, and in view of the support for these measures last night by the Leader of the Conservative Party (Mr. Clark) who, on previous occasions, admitted he would also retain the high interest rate policy of the Liberal government, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Beaches (Mr. Young):
That the Minister of Finance immediately offer his resignation to the Canadian people and, to be consistent with the Liberal-Conservative concept of sharing and solidarity, that the Leader of the Conservative Party also tender his resignation.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR MORATORIUM-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I, along with my fellow Canadians, am disappointed with the horrendous budgetary deficit projection of $19.6 billion plus and the disconcerting failure of the federal government to curb its own spending. Federal government demands on the borrowing market cannot have other than an inflationary effect on interest rates generally. This government has a double standard, one for the taxpayer and another for itself. It was delinquent in not ferreting out spending cuts which become obvious, extravagant foreign aid giveaways, language programs, rising executive staffs, the metric program, plus $5 million worth of firecrackers. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson):
That since Alberta has become the fourth province to exhibit formally its opposition to the forced metric program, by moving to assist Calgary resident Mrs. Kasparian, who has been charged because she used imperial, the government declare a moratorium on advancing the forced metric program, thereby saving at least $10 million this year alone in federal overhead costs and countless millions to retailers and consumers who will be hardest hit by the forced program.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: THE BUDGET-INDEXATION OF INCOME TAXES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance, who has just had his third strike, and in any honest or honourable government would be out by now. We have had the reaction of the market and the dollar to his budget. The dollar is sliding; the market is slumping dramatically. A lot of Canadians do not yet understand that last night, among other

June 29, 1982
Oral Questions
things, they had a massive tax increase imposed upon them of an average of $100 per taxpayer, at least.
The November budget, part of which still remains, talked a great deal about equity. I wonder if the Minister of Finance could tell us what has happened to that concept of equity, when he is forcing millions of lower and middle-income Canadians into higher tax brackets, by his changes in the indexation proposal, while those with incomes above $50,000 per year will continue to pay the same rates? Why in these massive new tax increases is he socking it to lower and middle-income Canadians, and why is he sparing the rich?

subsubtopic: THE BUDGET-INDEXATION OF INCOME TAXES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: THE BUDGET-INDEXATION OF INCOME TAXES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would just say in reply to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition that the concept of sharing is fully evident in the budget provisions. In the budget, it is true that we have asked certain Canadians to yield some of their benefits in order to help Canadians who are out of work or unemployed or who are faced with the loss of their homes or their businesses. We believe that it is reasonable in these circumstances to ask Canadians who are employed to share with those who are unemployed, so that we all can get through this difficult situation in a spirit of equity and sharing. That is the principle underlying the budget.

subsubtopic: THE BUDGET-INDEXATION OF INCOME TAXES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the problem with the minister's answer is that some Canadians share more than others. Lower and middle-income Canadians are being asked by this government to share, in the minister's words, more of the burden than are the rich. That does not meet any standard of equity which the country can recognize. Let me come to a particular group of Canadians who are being asked, if I might use the minister's word, to yield certain of their benefits. Even taking account of the changes in the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the 1.2 million Canadians who are receiving the old age pension will have their benefits, that they could have counted on, reduced because of the minister's action last night.
That is not true.
That is to say, 1.2 million elderly Canadians will be affected. Liberal members opposite say that is not true; I suggest that they read the budget, before they say that.
Hear, hear!
Let me ask the Minister of Finance why the elderly are singled out to pay for this government's mistakes?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I first want to underline to the Leader of the Opposition that the purpose of the
whole strategy of the government is to bring down the economy-
To its knees.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
-from a high level of inflation, at present very close to 12 per cent, to 6 per cent. If the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition and others in the country join in this national campaign to reduce inflation to 6 per cent, the incomes of those persons about whom he speaks will suffer very little damage, or the damage will be minimized, so there is a basic incentive for all Canadians to move to the 6 per cent level, if their concern is about the impact of the cap either on the personal income tax side or upon old age security.
However, it is vitally important to underline that no recipient of the old age pension who is in need is affected by this particular provision. It is the attempt of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition to instil anxiety in the minds of our senior citizens. I want to give the absolute assurance that no pensioner in need will be affected in any way by these measures.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, either the minister will amend his budget, or he is not telling the truth. The minister refuses to tell us why his tax proposals of last night spare the rich and hit low and middle-income Canadians, and why he is imposing special taxes upon 1.2 million elderly Canadians. He refuses to tell us why they are being singled out.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, why is the minister continuing the tax upon Blue Cross contributions, upon dental care provisions, and upon other employee benefits?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Including northern benefits.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition has again repeated that we are putting a special tax on the elderly. That is totally false.
Madam Speaker, once again we hear no answers from the Minister of Finance, who is taxing low-income Canadians, taxing middle-income Canadians, taxing the elderly, and sparing the rich.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: LEVEL OF PREMIUM RATE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, let me turn to the Minister of Employment and
June 29, 1982

Immigration. Since last night's budget shows an $800 million increase in the take from unemployment insurance premiums next year, can the minister tell the House how large an increase he is contemplating in this hidden tax which the Minister of Finance failed to mention last night?

subsubtopic: LEVEL OF PREMIUM RATE

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I too want to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. The meanest move in his budget last night was to reduce sharply the indexing of old age security for those who do not receive the supplement. In other words, that means that an elderly person who receives just over $8,000 a year in total income-which is what the minister receives every month- will receive $100 less next year, thanks to the minister. subsubtopic: EFFECT OF BUDGET ON OLD AGE PENSION BENEFITS

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF BUDGET ON UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Finance. Last night we had a no hope budget, with reduced pensions, reduced family allowances and taxes increased by more than $1 billion. If the backbenchers opposite will be quiet I would like to put my question to the Minister of Finance. Considering that all of this will take money out of the economy and lead to more bankruptcies, and more losses of jobs, will the minister confirm what one of his senior officials said during the lockup last night, namely, that unemployment in Canada, which is already at a disastrous high level, will remain virtually unchanged throughout this year?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT SCHEDULED OIL PRICE INCREASE BE POSTPONED
REQUEST THAT SCHEDULED OIL PRICE INCREASE BE POSTPONED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have another question about one of the main concerns of ordinary Canadians, namely, inflation. Considering that the thrust of the budget, according to the minister, was to bring down inflation, and considering that not one price increase was stopped and not one rollback took place, my question this time is to the Prime Minister who will be meeting with the First Ministers tomorrow.
On Thursday oil prices are scheduled to go up 10 per cent at the wellhead, which increase will lead to a 1 per cent rise in the cost of living and 22,000 fewer jobs in Canada. At that meeting will the Prime Minister urge the premiers of the producing provinces to forgo, along with the federal government, the 10 per cent increase on Thursday?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT SCHEDULED OIL PRICE INCREASE BE POSTPONED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I first want to thank the Leader of the New Democratic Party for having recognized in posing his question that there will be no decrease, as seems to have been alleged, in old age pensions and that there will be an increase-not as large as might otherwise have been expected, but there will be an increase, not a decrease, and I thank him for having put the record straight on that.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT SCHEDULED OIL PRICE INCREASE BE POSTPONED
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: REQUEST THAT SCHEDULED OIL PRICE INCREASE BE POSTPONED
speechtext: As regards the price of petroleum at the wellhead, the hon. member knows that price was reached after long and arduous discussions between the producing provinces and the federal government. I would be happy to carry the representations of the hon. member to the premiers tomorrow, but naturally that is not an area in which we can assert jurisdiction alone. It is a negotiated agreement which, incidentally, was adhered to by the former New Democratic Premier of Saskatchewan. I repeat, I would be happy to carry that representation to them, but 1 certainly would not want to indicate that the federal government alone would go back on that contractual arrangement.

Madam Speaker, so that we are perfectly clear on this point, the agreement, as the Prime Minister knows, was negotiated late last summer or into the fall and, as this whole country knows, things have changed considerably for the worse since then. Is the Prime Minister saying to the House, on behalf of the federal government, that in his meeting with the premiers tomorrow he is prepared to forgo the federal government's share of that proposed increase? I would like him to make that very clear, and in so doing will he be then saying to the premiers and the oil industry that he expects them to do the same so that at last we can have some concrete action which will be a positive step to reducing inflation in this country?
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I find the suggestion a little bit bewildering because for months the New Democratic Party, indeed the members of the official opposition, argued that what this country needed was the certainty and security of knowing what the prices would be. The hon. member knows that not only were those prices reached after long and arduous negotiation, but in some cases there was a refusal to continue production by the producing provinces. He knows that the agreement meant prices for Canadian consumers substantially below world prices, and I do not see it as being in the public interest to reopen that contract at this time.
I can understand the suggestion now made by the Leader of the New Democratic Party, but I think he has to bear in mind the some 18 months of difficulty during which these negotiations took place. He has to bear in mind the consequences of the Alsands project being stalled and eventually stopped for that period of time, the consequences of the fact that eastern Canadian refiners and importers had to sign contracts for offshore oil, and the consequences due to the fact that therefore a lot of the production was shut-in in Alberta and Saskatchewan. I do not think that I can, simply on the basis of a question, now say that these 18 months of arduous negotiations will be swept away just because the Leader of the New Democratic Party has a suggestion in mind.
June 29, 1982

Madam Speaker,
I am pleased to see that the Prime Minister has finally admitted that the energy negotiation delays were the key factor in the cancellation of the Alsands project. He never admitted that before, and now we know.
I have a very simple question for the Prime Minister regarding pensions of senior citizens. Will he explain to this House how a pensioner is better off when inflation is up 11 per cent, as is projected, and his pension cheque will be up only 6 per cent?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF BUDGET
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in so far as what the hon. member calls an admission about the cancellation of the tar sands is concerned, I do not think he has to feign surprise in that regard. It is certain that for a period of many months the federal Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was saying that we were prepared to go ahead with the tar sands. He said this in answer to many questions in this House, and the hon. member knows that the answer was that the Premier of Alberta said that he would not go ahead with the tar sands unless the whole energy agreement was settled. Therefore, the stalling on the Alsands was not by the federal government; we had made the concessions needed there. The reason why they did not proceed 18 months before was because the Premier of Alberta, as is his right, wanted to look at negotiations as a whole package. That is the reason why Alsands did not proceed earlier.
In so far as the question on pensions is concerned, Madam Speaker, I am afraid the Minister of Finance did not succeed in convincing the opposition of what is behind this whole budget when he talks of a 6 per cent future. I am confident the people of Canada will have got the message and that they, and many of the economic decision makers in this country, the businessmen and even labour leaders, will be prepared to recognize that it is in our interest to bring inflation down to 6 per cent next year. If we can do it-and we can only do it collectively-there will be no reduction even in the speed of the increase in old age pensions. Six per cent is what they will get, 6 per cent will be the CPI if we have co-operation-

speechtext:

speechtext: Madam Speaker, one of the other very important concerns of Canadians is the question of high interest rates. The federal government budgetary deficit of $20 billion is clearly a major obstacle to achieving low interest rates, and when you combine that with the $44 billion of government debt coming due between now and the end of the year, the obstacle is almost insurmountable. What measures is the minister proposing to lead this country to a lower level of interest rates in the face of those two obstacles?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR TAX INCENTIVES FOR INDUSTRY
REQUEST FOR TAX INCENTIVES FOR INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Today the stock market dropped like a stone because the minister has failed to recognize that this country faces a full-scale financial crisis. Major corporate bankruptcies are pending because companies are staggering under their debt load and they cannot generate cash to keep their doors open. Instead of bringing in major tax savings and tax incentives, the minister is proposing to consult with industry over the next few months on a variety of proposals, which is like consulting with a home owner whose house is burning down on whether to get a pail of water.
Why does the minister not introduce tax incentives and savings incentives now, immediately, when the economy desperately needs them? Why is the minister waiting until later when all these companies will be broke and the jobs will be lost?

June 29, 1982
Oral Questions

subtopic: REQUEST FOR TAX INCENTIVES FOR INDUSTRY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in the past we have heard the Minister of Finance explain how our economic troubles are the fault of U.S. policy or are the fault of policies in Europe. Now I suppose he will say it is the stock market's fault for wiping $2.5 billion from the value of stocks because of his budget.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is also for the Minister of Finance. The November 12 budget slapped an additional tax increase on construction and resource industry workers by taxing their job-related expenses, such as health and dental plans, transportation, and room and board. In British Columbia these tax increases amount to about $3 an hour for each worker. How can the minister expect these workers, who were hit with these tax increases only seven months ago, to limit their wage demands to 6 per cent? Why does the Minister of Finance not remove these unfair taxes if he really expects workers in the resource and construction industries to accept these kinds of limits?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I believe that the choice I stated last night is very clear. If Canadians generally want to live in a world of recession they will insist upon wage settlements and income demands of 11 and 12 per cent. Demand your resignation.

speechtext: -take steps to reduce these income demands. You are having as much trouble as you had in November.
You could help by resigning.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF BUDGET
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Prior to last evening the major problems that confronted Canadian families were high interest rates, high unemployment, the large deficit of the government, and inflation. speechtext: Right on.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF BUDGET
speechtext: We will not have as much money in the economy as a result of the government's determination to extract $1.3 billion in additional tax revenue from Canadians. speechtext:

June 29, 1982

homes, but also to buyers of existing homes. 1 believe that is assistance to the home owner and also to the construction industry.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF PURCHASE GRANTS ON MORTGAGE PAYMENTS
