The Budget-Mr. Epp

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On the Peace Tower in this building, engraved in stone, is the statement: "Without vision the people perish." Without the vision of government, without the leadership, do not talk to me about the fact that you like government, that you are comfortable in the government benches. Talk to me about how you will lead Canadians, how you will give them vision once again. Because only as we are going to have economic development, economic success, will the matters of social justice again become valid in this House and in this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Only then. You cannot talk about social justice until such a moment as you give economic opportunity. Too many of us have people back in the Soviet Union. They hear a lot about social justice; they see very little of economic development as individuals, and so it becomes empty.
So, the first thing that has to happen, Mr. Speaker, is for this government to understand that it, and it first-not others, it-holds first responsibility to the economic crisis that we find ourselves in as Canadians. Should that happen, I think we would then be able to start on the road to recovery.
Canadians today are afraid. I said that today I was sad. Possibly people hearing me would say I am more angry than sad. I am both. But there is a myth that has gone through the Canadian public consciousness. I did not live in that period of time, but coming out of the 1930s there was an apology that "Tory times are tough times."

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They still are.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) still believes that. There was the mythology, though, on the other side of that coin, that no matter what the Liberal Party did to you, they were good economic managers. Take a look at them now, Mr. Speaker. Any management expertise they might have had, any management reputation they might have developed at some time, surely has broken like shards at their feet. And the people who are most disappointed are Canadians.
We hear about the deficit. Jocularly, almost, they say: "We must do something about the deficit, it is serious, we have to do something." Let us look at the deficit. 1 remember a few weeks ago when there were rumours that the deficit was going to be substantially higher than the $10.9 billion projected in the November 12 budget. There were members in the House and commentators who were saying that the budget could almost go all the way up to $15 billion, maybe to $16 billion, and in some quarters some members were saying: "Oh, do you think it could go that high, do you think it could any higher?" None of us dared believe that the deficit could approach $20 billion. That $20 billion-or $19.6 billion-is projected on two other matters which the government does not want to talk about, and that is this: one, what will be the shortfall in the unemployment insurance fund-which we will know at the end of the third quarter, that will be January 1983. It could be, most likely, another $2 billion. Plus, the minister is banking
that the deficit will not go any higher because he is planning that there will be growth in the next two quarters. Does any Canadian who has looked at the situation today believe that we will have that kind of growth in the next quarter? Can you show me one reputable economist or investor who believes that? And this is the smoke and mirrors that the minister likes to play with. Somehow he feels that the light of truth will simply not sear away those words that he is so quick to use.
With respect to the deficit of $20 billion plus, there is no other single factor which will more quickly, more dramatically or more deeply erode confidence in our country than that deficit. If hon. members opposite individually were spending 33 per cent annually more than they earned, how long would their families survive? How long would they sit around their breakfast tables as families and make plans for the future? Is that the legacy they are leaving to Canadians?
I know there are many Canadians who have invested in Canada savings bonds. Last September the bond issue came out at 19 per cent plus. In my mind, at least, the setting of that rate set a target for interest rates for the next year. Why should a Canadian invest in Canadian business if he is guaranteed 19 per cent plus without risk?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How much did you pay?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member opposite wants to be personal. He can do that, but I point out that the only way we are going to get our economy back in line is by rewarding risk-takers to a greater extent than we reward bond holders. What will be the rate for the bond issue this year? Is that a factor in the deficit? The government has to get into the bond market. It has to get $20 billion, and the more it can find domestically the better.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They need $60 billion.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
With the rollovers the government needs $60 billion, but to get that what offer does the government have to make to Canadians, with inflation running at the rate it is today? What offer does the government have to make to Canadians, and what will be the cost? That is the legacy of hon. members opposite.
An interesting exchange took place in the House of Commons today during the question period. It was a rather sad exchange about old age security. The government was hanging on to the fact that old age security payments for next year would go up-not down-and from a strictly dollar point of view, that is correct. If OAS is to be inflated by 6 per cent, obviously the payments will be higher than they are this year. That is fair enough argument for the government to make. However, at no point was the government willing to concede that the amount pensioners will receive will be less than what they expected in terms of meeting inflation and the erosion of their buying power next year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A heartless government.
June 29, 1982

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) likes to champion causes and create the image that she is always there working for the less fortunate in our society. She said the government would give pensioners $10 per month more. They will get $239 this year and $249 next year. Let us examine that for a moment. These are the people who were our pioneers. These are the people whose salaries almost invariably were substantially lower than salaries earned today-by those of us who have work. They are the people who saved for that time when they would be senior citizens. Is it valid to give them that kind of sleight of hand argument? Is it valid to give them smoke and mirrors and to say that, because it is more, they therefore should not ask for an explanation as to why it would otherwise be less?
The government is asking for confidence. The government wants the economy to start rolling. If that is the goal and that is the sincere aim, I say in all sincerity that the government should tell Canadians the whole story and not hold back that which might not be favourable. Only then will the government gain some credibility.
I also found it interesting that the hon. member for Don Valley East (Mr. Smith) blamed the media for the government's problems. He said the media had created a hype. At the time of the Meach Lake experience the government went to the mountain top. I suppose the members of the government wanted to get some revelation-perhaps not equal to the Ten Commandments, but some revelation nonetheless.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Water.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If they went for water, that would have been better. After Meach Lake the response of members of the government to any questions in the House was, "Wait for Versailles, wait for Versailles." The response was that when the minister returned from Versailles-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We never said that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nonsense.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Was that not said?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No. Name one who did.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will name one: the Minister of Finance.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Pierre Trudeau.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Or the Prime Minsiter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What did he say?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then after Versailles the response was, "Wait for the economic statement", which became a budget. Hon. members opposite can blame the media all they want. Some days I take a certain jaundiced view of the media myself, but let hon. members be honest; they used every one of those events to hold off the inevitable, which came last night in the budget.
How can we turn the economy around? Is it possible? I believe it is because of our potential as a country. Tomorrow
The Budget-Mr. Epp
there will be what I suppose I can call a federal-provincial conference. There will be a meeting of the Prime Minister with the ten premiers of the country. The Prime Minister has told them, "We must co-operate." That is true, but when we look at the events of the past 18 months, can we say that the Prime Minsiter is the best person to preach co-operation in Canadian federalism?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He said co-operative federalism is dead.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I believe in co-operative federalism.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are not the judge of that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Fair enough, but the Prime Minister said cooperative federalism is dead.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who are you to judge that?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am telling the hon. member what the Prime Minister said. What happened with the EPF? What happened in the constitutional debate? The Prime Minister said cooperative federalism is dead. How can he expect, after one short post-budget meeting tomorrow, that suddenly cooperation will be natural? The Prime Minister himself said today that the energy agreement with Alberta and Saskatchewan took 18 months to achieve. What about the Atlantic offshore problem?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the budget?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: These are all factors in tomorrow's meeting. Granted, we are in very difficult times and need co-operative federalism, but this Prime Minister is the only Prime Minister in the history of the country who has had such an abysmal record in dealing with the provinces.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On account of you guys. On account of you, trouble-makers.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I note the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau), who was the chairman of a committee which made a report which was totally annihilated and destroyed by the Minister of Finance, is in the House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You haven't read the report.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the hon. member for Gloucester wants to speak, he can ask his whip. His whip might even let him speak next year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tomorrow at five o'clock.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is there any other factor? I believe that if we return to co-operative federalism, in time confidence can be restored. However, the federal government will have to recognize that the provinces are partners in federalism and that they have a role to play. That role should not simply be to answer a call by the Prime Minister to come to Ottawa 48 hours after the budget to be told, "That is what you will do, or else." The Prime Minister has taken that approach too often.

June 29, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Malepart
There are other aspects of the budget that I should like to touch upon. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) spoke about the housing program, but, Mr. Speaker, to date every program he has brought forward has fallen well short of his projections. Now we hear about a $3,000 grant for first time home buyers and, on the face of it, it is a step in the right direction. It could increase house building, construction jobs and jobs in the subtrades. But let us analyse this, Mr. Speaker.
A family in Winnipeg buying a basic house at a cost of approximately $60,000 would have to put 10 per cent down under this plan. With their $7,000 and the $3,000 grant, they are left with a mortgage of $50,000. It does not take long to figure how much interest that young couple must pay, at 18 per cent. In the first twelve months, when they receive the $3,000, their interest payment, taxes and upkeep will amount to $9,000.
The government is in charge of one of the richest countries in the world, Mr. Speaker. We can turn this country around but, first of all, the government must come clean with the people. It has perpetrated a disaster on the country. The next election will put it back in its place and that is, out of office. Unfortunately, future generations will have to shoulder the deficit it has created.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take part in the debate on the budget brought down yesterday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). Mr. Speaker, I sincerely believe, considering the difficult economic situation facing all industrialized countries, that the budget tabled by the Minister of Finance is a good budget and a realistic one, because it pursues two important objectives, namely to fight unemployment and inflation. The opposition parties, both the Progressive Conservative and the New Democratic Party, will say that it is not enough or that it is too little, too late, but if we look at this budget, still bearing in mind the economic situation and from a realistic rather than a political point of view, we must admit that it is a realistic budget, and I am confident that the measures announced in this budget will make a positive contribution towards helping Canadians who are facing problems at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, looking at the measures announced in the budget that will provide assistance to the unemployed, homeowners who are being squeezed by high mortgage rates, farmers, fishermen and small businesses, we shall see that the programs have met the expectations of Canadians. In fact, the government will spend $1.4 billion on financial assistance for these groups and on job creation.
And just how, Mr. Speaker, does the government intend to fight unemployment? First of all, the government will inject $200 million into local development programs which are
extremely important, not only for job creation but also for the kind of services they set up for Canadians in ridings across the country. In addition, the government will spend $300 million on economic development programs in the private sector for the creation of permanent jobs. Both types of programs will ensure that additional jobs are created quickly and targeted especially to areas which have been particularly hard hit by the recession. Mr. Speaker, the government has decided to fight unemployment by creating jobs through housing assistance programs. The minister has announced five major measures to respond to the needs of the housing sector, while at the same time creating employment. The following is a passage related to the first program, and I quote:
The government will provide grants of $3,000 to all purchasers of new houses on which construction starts before December 31, 1982, and to first-time buyers who purchase an existing house before that date. It is estimated that 100,000 purchasers will be eligible for this grant. The total cost of this new program is $300 million.
Under the second program, the government will add an additional $30 million allocation to the home renovation plan, thus increasing it to $60 million. Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday I had an opportunity to meet with Montreal representatives of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and city of Montreal officials, and I can assure the House that the program is greatly appreciated by the people of Montreal and that there are many applications, and I congratulate the minister on having given this program his special attention.
The third program also recognizes the needs of low-income Canadians. Under the program, the number of co-operative housing units will be increased by 2,500, thus raising the total number from 25,000 to 27,500 in 1982, in recognition of the housing needs of low-income groups. To demonstrate the importance of co-operative housing programs, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote a letter from a member of a co-operative in my riding. I must say that in 1981 I saw 843 housing units under construction and, recently, I had the opportunity to attend the opening ceremonies of a co-operative which has managed to recycle or use an abandoned school and convert it into housing units. I can assure the House that the 31 families now living in those units built under the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation assistance program have nothing but praise for the minister's decision. I should like to quote a letter from someone in my riding who belongs to the co-operative movement:
Sir:
As a voter in the Sainte-Marie riding, Mr. Malepart, I want to congratulate you for supporting the co-operative formula. I should think that you will gain more support if additional units are built. Having lived through that experiment in the past two years, I can assure you that the formula ought to be put forward. Unlike the low rental housing alternative, it gives tenants a sense of autonomy; people residing in co-operative units talk to each other, contribute to the chores to be done, which promotes dialogue and security. The units are very well maintained and the rent is reasonable, which is why I joined the movement because I have a small income and I could hardly make ends meet. This housing unit formula was just what I needed and I am sure I was not the only one in that predicament. I am a member of a Quebec association for the protection of the
June 29, 1982

rights of people who are retired or about to be and I want to assure you that I am interested in anything that has to do with housing and I follow all programs very closely. Keep up the good work.
Yours truly,
Marie-Paule Langlois,
President
Rosemont Boulevard Co-operative Housing
Mr. Speaker, when people write letters like that, I think that one should stop criticizing-naturally, being permanently in the official opposition does account for a negative approach- and that after a series of programs such as that one, the Minister of Finance is to be congratulated. The programs which I have just mentioned should provide some 65,000 jobs during the next two years. I think that it is important. Moreover, the government is prepared to show some flexibility about the rental support plan which provides interest-free loans of $7,500. The government is prepared to increase that amount in some areas. It should be remembered that last March that plan was increased to 30,000 rental units and the creation of 50,000 additional jobs is anticipated. And I should add that this is another program of which the representatives from Montreal are proud and wish to make extensive use. Mr. Speaker, the Minister announced that the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan introduced last November will be extended to December 31, 1983. Thus all home owners having to spend more than 30 per cent of their gross income on their mortgage payment, as a result of a renewal taking place after last evening, will be eligible for a grant of up to $3,000. It will no longer be necessary to defer interest before becoming eligible for a grant.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the constituents of Montreal-Sainte-Marie will be pleased to take advantage of those housing and job-creation programs. I should like to mention that after consultation with my nine other colleagues from eastern Montreal, we asked for job-creation programs through housing construction and direct assistance to business. This was done after consultation with the people of eastern Montreal during a four-day tour on economic issues. Mr. Speaker, the minister also announced the injection of $500 million for interest assistance to small businesses, farmers and fishermen. This will reduce plant closures and job losses. Those are, Mr. Speaker, important steps to fight unemployment.
Now let us see the steps taken by the government to bring down inflation, an evil affecting everyone but especially small and middle-income Canadians. We must remember that the minister has asked all Canadians to work together to bring down inflation, but that he insisted on protecting low-income Canadians, including middle-income families receiving family allowances and the child tax credit and senior citizens who receive the guaranteed income supplement. As its first antiinflation measure, the government has decided to cut pay
The Budget-Mr. Malepart
increases to 6 per cent for the next year and to 5 per cent the year after for employees in the federal public sector.
The first affected will be members of the House of Commons, ministers of the Crown and senators. In addition to restricting salary increases to 6 per cent next year and to 5 per cent the following year, the minister has announced that our salaries will be reduced this year. In addition, pay increases for public servants and Crown corporation employees will be limited to the same targets of 6 per cent and 5 per cent for the next two years. Moreover, the government will limit the indexation of personal exemptions and tax brackets to 6 per cent for the 1983 taxation year and to 5 per cent for the 1984 taxation year. Effective January 1, 1983, indexation of the pensions paid to former Members of Parliament and public servants will be limited to 6 per cent for 12 months and to 5 per cent for the following 12 months. Effective the same dates, the indexing factor applicable to family allowances and old age security pensions will also be limited to 6 per cent and 5 per cent for the next 2 years.
However, Mr. Speaker, I am glad to note that the Minister of Finance has protected low income families by increasing by $50 the child tax credit for the 1982 taxation year which will continue to be fully indexed. This increase will raise the credit from $293 to $343 for each child. I believe that this decision is much fairer than that made by the Parti Quebecois government in Quebec on January 1, which was to grant no increase in family allowances, and I would like to remind my Progressive Conservative friends in this regard that when they were in power, they had created a committee to remove the universality principle from the family allowance program. Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the minister for protecting senior citizens receiving the guaranteed income supplement in part or in full, which will continue to be fully indexed. Then again the Minister of Finance did not follow the example set by the Levesque government when they decided, on January 1, to index social benefits at 8 per cent rather than the amount of indexing, and in the case of mothers with children to index at 6 per cent only. He provided instead for increases in the federal family allowances and tax credit. I would also tell my Progressive Conservative friends that as far as the basic pension is concerned, they themselves had a committee looking into the abolition of universal pensions, let alone limiting indexation to 6 per cent. They should be honest in their comments today. Also, veterans' pensions will remain fully indexed.
Mr. Speaker, in order to fight inflation, the Canadian government is not content with limiting salary increases. It is also asking federal agencies that regulate the cost of essential goods and services, such as public transportation, public communications and food, to endorse the objects of this budget and to limit price increases. In addition, the Prime Minister will meet tomorrow with provincial premiers. He will ask them to limit price increases as well within their jurisdiction, and I hope they will agree to that.

June 29, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Deans
Mr. Speaker, the budget also includes a new interesting proposal to consider implementing a special program of interest rates lowered by 3 to 6 per cent for buyers of new homes. Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, this budget puts foward significant proposals to fight unemployment and inflation, and I am convinced that all my constituents in my Montreal-Sainte-Marie riding will make maximum use of these new assistance programs. I will make it a duty to help them get more, because I am convinced that Canadians across the country will use the programs made available by the Canadian government, despite the criticism voiced by the Progressive Conservatives and the New Democrats.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 am certainly pleased to have an opportunity to speak on this budget. I will not begin the major part of my speech now since there is only a minute or two left. I wonder if it might be considered ten o'clock in order that I could commence fresh tomorrow.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Fine. Then let me deal very briefly with the remarks of the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) who devoted much of his time to putting on the record matters which were blatantly unsupportable by the facts. I want to make it quite clear that his comments were not only unkind and unjustified, they were untrue. I would suggest that if the hon. member were to be as honourable as he claims to be, he would be prepared to come into the House and retract many of the statements he made. However, knowing the calibre and quality of much of the comment made by the official opposition, I am quite sure he would not want to do that.
I want to put very quickly, sir, one matter on the record. A lot has been said about the deficit, and it is true the deficit has reached a level which must surely be causing every single member of the House of Commons great alarm. However, if we continue with the policies set out in the budget document presented to us by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on Monday evening, there is no doubt in my mind that the deficit we have today is but a pittance compared to the deficit we are going to have within the next year.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-PUBLICITY ISSUED BY MONTREAL FESTIVAL

speechtext:
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, on June 21 I put a question to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) with respect to an ad
which appeared in the Montreal Gazette on June 19. This was an ad published by the Festival du Vieux Port de Montreal, a federal Crown corporation which reports to parliament through the Minister of Public Works. This ad which was completely in the French language was published in an English-language newspaper, namely The Gazette, in a city where 20 per cent of the population is English speaking.
In my question I asked the minister why this ad was published in French in violation and in contradiction of the Federal Officials Languages Act and in violation of the provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in those sections dealing with language rights. 1 asked the minister to investigate why this ad had been published in such contravention and in such an insensitive way. I asked the minister what he would do to correct this situation. He responded that he had not been aware of the situation but he felt that it was an insensitive act on the part of those who did it and that he would look into the matter.
Following that answer in the House 1 learned through the press, not directly through my office, that the reason the ad was published only in French is that an English version had not yet been prepared. I do not think that is an acceptable reason. I might point out as well that all other publicity materials published by the federal Crown corporation Festival du Vieux Port de Montreal were also published solely and completely in the French language. I have here an invitation to a reception to announce the summer program of the festival. It is in French only. I have another invitation from Mr. Paul Gerin-Lajoie, president of the Crown corporation, with respect to another opening ceremony, which is completely in French. When the ad was finally put in the Montreal Gazette in English on June 26 a so-called translated ad was printed with some terrible mistakes in the English language. For example they translated the French which read: "Programmation a diviser et a conserver" as "unscrew and save". In other words I was to unscrew this from the Montreal Gazette and save it. I do not believe there is any excuse to violate the federal Official Languages Act in English or in French anywhere in this country.
This is not the first time I have complained about the federal public service in Quebec operating solely in French. I have done so before, and I have complained with respect to billboard programs only in French in parts of Montreal where the population is 80 per cent English-speaking. I have complained about places where federal public servants in Quebec refuse to speak English to English-speaking clients in the city of Montreal. It is my belief that the federal government through its ministers must make clear to the public service in Quebec that we operate in both official languages and that we serve the public in the official language of their choice.
June 29, 1982

In 1977 the federal government made it clear in a published statement that the federal government does not come under the provisions of Bill 101 in Quebec. Bill 101 is a provincial law covering provincial matters and a provincial responsibility. All matters in Quebec that come under federal responsibility are subject to the bilingual provision of the federal law on that subject matter.
I might say that since my question was raised in the House the federal government has published a full page ad in the Montreal Gazette about which I was extremely pleased. This confirmed the federal government's policy on official languages. This ad is titled, "The Government of Canada Serving You in Both Official Languages in Your Area". It sets out all the departments in Montreal and where you can complain if there is any violation of language rights in the Montreal area. That is the sort of policy I want to see but it must be maintained in every area of the public service in Quebec and throughout Canada.
I also want to make it clear that I am not opposed to any measure which will fully protect and help the French language in Quebec flourish. However, one language is not helped by bringing punitive measures against another language, especially a minority language. I might also add that actions such as these by federal civil servants in Quebec are occurring at a time when there is a provincial government which is continually eroding minority rights of English speaking people in the province of Quebec. Therefore, this action, when added to the sins of the other government, are not well received.
I am pleased with this follow-up ad which was put in The Gazette on June 23 setting out our policy on official languages, but I want to urge very strongly that the government ensure that all their directors and top civil servants in Quebec are made fully aware of our policy on official languages in Quebec, and to ensure that the population of that province is served in the official language of choice, be it English or French, and that the same policy be pursued throughout the country with respect to the French language minorities in other provinces.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Mr. Henri Tousignant (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-PUBLICITY ISSUED BY MONTREAL FESTIVAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to reply tonight to the question the hon. member raised in the House on June 21. The minister had promised then to look into the matter. I understand that the minister has asked the officials of the Festival du Vieux Port de Montreal to provide him with detailed information concerning the publication of an ad completely in French in the English-speaking Montreal Gazette. The Festival du Vieux Port de Montreal is a federal Crown corporation which is listed in Schedule C of the Financial Administration Act and which reports to Parliament through the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove). It was established in 1981 to update the waterfront in old Montreal.
Adjournment Debate
Its purpose is to promote, administer and develop the waterfront. It must comply with the Government of Canada's official language policy and, as a matter of fact, has always complied with them. It is unfortunate that the ad which was published in The Gazette of June 19 was in French only. This ad was designed to promote the Festival du Vieux Port this summer which was scheduled to begin on June 20. In view of the tight publicity schedule and last-minute changes to the French version, it was decided to publish the ad anyway to make sure that The Gazette readership would be aware of the event. On June 26, as the hon. member has just mentioned the ad was published again, in English this time, in The Gazette and the Ottawa Citizen.
Of course, errors will happen as they often do in French translation. I would also emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that this is an exceptional case, even a unique one. I want to assure hon. members that every effort will be made to ensure that the Canadian government's policy on official languages is strictly adhered to by the corporation of the Vieux Port de Montreal. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, 1 would take this opportunity to commend the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace- Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) for his perceptiveness and pay tribute to his continuing vigilance, either in this House or outside. He never hesitates to defend our policy on official languages. I hope he is satisfied with this information.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF LAYOFFS. (B) REQUEST THAT MINISTER MAKE REPRESENTATIONS TO CABINET
CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF LAYOFFS. (B) REQUEST THAT MINISTER MAKE REPRESENTATIONS TO CABINET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I rose in the House of Commons and asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to assure the 3,000 CN workers who were being laid off that they will indeed be rehired, and that the lay-offs are only temporary. I asked him to advise these workers when they will be rehired. At that time the minister advised that the lay-offs were until October 15, 1982. However, he did not say if they would all be rehired. This only leads to scared speculation, not reassurance.
1 would like to ask the minister a question: if not all of these
3,000	CN employees, 750 of whom live in the Moncton area, are not rehired, where does the minister expect them to find alternative employment? In the Moncton area there is little hope they would find suitable employment because there are no jobs available. Much of the credit for this must go to the federal government.
Many of the actions initiated by this government and by the minister himself have cost the maritimes and the Moncton area thousands of jobs, jobs that are desperately needed and that simply cannot be found. In the past year the government is responsible for terminating the Atlantic Limited with the loss of hundreds of jobs and millions in revenues. This decision was taken on one of Canada's most popular and best used

June 29, 1982
Adjournment Debate
passenger trains. It is responsible for transferring the water quality control out of Moncton to Brampton, Ontario, thereby terminating several more jobs. It is undoubtedly responsible for the odious and questionable decision to close down CFB Chatham. This closure will cost the community 1,500 jobs and $30 million annually in lost revenues. CFB Chatham contributes over 40 per cent of basic employment in the Miramichi region. This is a move that will reverberate all the way to Moncton. This government is also responsible for postponing the multi-million dollar Mitel project.
Now, any hope that had been held to improve the Atlantic economy and relieve the massive unemployment of this region has been shattered by a budget that has completely ignored this rampant problem. The finance minister failed again to find an answer to the severe economic retardation and spiralling unemployment that afflicts Atlantic Canada. This region has the highest unemployment of any region in Canada-14.5 per cent-and it promises to get worse. In fact, all indicators suggest that the recent budget could very well aggravate the unemployment problem.
There is an alternative to these lay-offs; a very feasible and constructive alternative to these unwanted and apparently unnecessarily long lay-offs. The CN employees who are being laid off could well be kept on to maintain and repair the rail equipment and prepare it for the time when business is better. This is a policy supported and advocated by the CN employees who are eager and anxious to work.
A great deal of CN equipment is not being properly maintained and a slow period such as we are in would be an ideal time to repair and maintain the rolling stock as well as the tracks, bridges etc. Three bad derailments have occurred in the past eight months in the maritime region that are directly attributable to the poor condition of either the rolling stock or the beds. Human error was not responsible. These derailments cost millions of dollars in clean-up operations, lost cargo and lost equipment. Those same dollars could better and more safely be used to keep men working to maintain this equipment at peak condition.
If the men were kept working to maintain this equipment CN would be in a better position to handle increased goods when business improves. I trust they will not allow themselves to be caught in a position of having to turn away business because they do not have the equipment needed to handle the job. That is simply bad management.
I have a telegram I received from the New Brunswick Federation of Labour advising me of a motion passed by its brotherhood unanimously condemning plans by CN and CP railways to further extend the length of the earlier announced closure of the main shops. In the telegram the Federation says:
These lay-offs will cause thousands of railway workers across Canada to be unemployed, further compounding an already disastrous unemployment situation. Federal Liberal government support of this action demonstrates a total disregard for the dignity of those workers affected who want to be a productive part of society.
The effects of these lay-offs will undoubtedly compound the problems afflicting the economy. These CN employees are
being told they will be laid off for 13 weeks. That is 3 months and one week. We are talking about three months and one week during which families are required to tighten their belts and live without incomes, whereby additional dollars would be forever lost to the business community. These people want to work; they are proud and independent. They want the 13 weeks of work and the assurance they will all have jobs. I am hoping that the callous and insensitive attitudes offered the Canadian public are not perpetuated in this situation too.
Last night the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) stole the last hope a great many Canadians had for economic recovery and for new jobs. Economists predict the situation will get worse before it gets better. The nonproductive and avoidable lay-off of 3,000 employees will not help this situation. It will only worsen the predicament.
The Minister of Transport has an opportunity here to aid 750 people in the Moncton area and another 2,300 across Canada in maintaining their jobs, and preserving their pride and dignity, and to keep the economy of these affected regions from becoming worse. I recommend that the Minister of Transport urge CN and CP to put these workers to work this summer maintaining the rail equipment. It is a job that has to be done, one these workers have the expertise to do and one that will allow rail employees the dignity of working and earning a living.
This government also has a responsibility to Canadians to ensure a prosperous economic environment. To borrow the words of the Minister of Finance:
Canadians want to know how we can get our economy growing again, how we can get industry to invest, expand and provide the jobs our people need. There are 1,250,000 among us who are unemployed. Still more are struggling to make ends meet in the face of high inflation and interest rates. We are all suffering one way or another from the recession that is battering our economy. We are all searching for a way out of it.
The minister continued to say that the purpose of his budget was to offer Canadians a way to end the recession and to speed our progress toward recovery through immediate action. As the government elected by Canadians to do the job, the ball is in their court. I suggest they get on with it. Recovery cannot be aided by laying off 3,000 rail employees.
It seems that this government is determined to ride to glory on the backs of pensioners, the armed services, and those productively employed. My position as a Member of Parliament requires that, despite the deaf ears and petrified minds 1 am attempting to appeal to, I must continue to appeal to those minds on behalf of the people of the Atlantic region of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-ANNOUNCEMENT OF LAYOFFS. (B) REQUEST THAT MINISTER MAKE REPRESENTATIONS TO CABINET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I compliment the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett) for speaking so strongly on behalf of the constituents in that part of the country. However, I would remind the hon. member that Canadian National must compete in the marketplace the same as any private industry.
June 29, 1982

It is faced with the same financial pressures in times of declining business activity as other Canadian companies, whether publicly or privately owned. If, as a Crown corporation, CN is asked to isolate itself from the marketplace, the government would be expected to provide financial assistance, and on a very large scale.
In response to last night's budget, the hon. member's party criticized this government viciously for the deplorable deficits, yet he did not recommend tonight how the government will pay CN to cover these workers. Let us have some constructive suggestions, not just willy-nilly criticisms.
The hon. member is aware, because the minister has pointed out in this House and I have pointed out previously in this chamber, that CN lost $67 million in the first quarter compared to a $70 million gain last year. Revenue tonne miles for the first five and a half months of 1982 were down almost 15 per cent. Carloadings were down 16 per cent at the end of May and 9,500 cars are sitting idle.
It is in this context that CN was forced to take the difficult decision of extending the regular close-down of maintenance shops. I emphasize that it is a close-down. The planned recall date is October 15.
In conclusion, I want to repeat what I and the minister have said, that most workers will be receiving up to 80 per cent of their salaries during the close-down period. I hope the hon. member will look at this particular situation in the context of what the Minister of Finance said last night. Only through the spirit of solidarity and sharing are we going to improve the situation and get these employees back to work.
When the hon. member tries to shoulder the blame on the government, I remind him that in a democratic system of government the opposition is part of that government. The opposition has a role to play, to remind Canadians that we have to put our shoulders together, and work together to bring down this 12 per cent recession to a 6 per cent recovery.

subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-DELAY IN ON-RESERVE HOUSING PROGRAM. (B) CONSTRUCTION OF SCHOOL AT DILLON, SASKATCHEWAN
INDIAN AFFAIRS-DELAY IN ON-RESERVE HOUSING PROGRAM. (B) CONSTRUCTION OF SCHOOL AT DILLON, SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the circumstances I want to bring up this evening have to do with questions I put to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) on June 16 during question period. As yet I have heard nothing in reply from the minister. I am very concerned. If I cannot get answers to these questions this evening from the hon. parliamentary secretary, I would like him to at least take time to prepare a response very soon on this pressing problem.
The Buffalo River Indian Band in Dillon, Saskatchewan is very concerned about a school which is soon to be built in their community. The band is located in a remote area of northern Saskatchewan. Because of their situation they appealed to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, asking that their school be built in accordance with provincial standards. Although it is not the case in all areas of Canada, it is a fact that in Saskatchewan standards set for building schools
Adjournment Debate
are far superior to the federal standard set by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
After pressing the minister the band received a commitment that the school would be built according to provincial standards, and as a result these would be a much better facility to meet the needs of the local citizens.
Now that the time for the construction of the new school has come upon us, it is suspected that the minister is being pressured by some department officials to back out of his commitment. Some questions need to be answered and I respectfully ask that they be answered now or fairly soon.
First, will the minister keep his commitment and see that the school for the Buffalo River Band will be built to provincial standards, or at least an updated federal equivalent, which could be the case? This would help many other Indian bands in Saskatchewan as well.
Second, I would like to know when this information will be communicated to the band officials.
Third, if there are any problems, will the minister meet with the band to solve them?
Finally, when will construction of the new school actually commence?
These questions need to be answered, and answered soon, so that the children at Dillon will not have to face another year of going to school in a building in such decrepit condition. Part of the national media last year covered the situation of the parents at Dillon, members of the Buffalo River Band, pulling their students out of school and not allowing them to go back until the government made a commitment to build a school for them. The conditions are very bad in the present school.
I see that my time is quickly passing, so I would like to pose a second question. It is a question dealing with the on-reserve housing program in the province of Saskatchewan. I imagine this not only applies to Saskatchewan but extends throughout Canada. I am familiar with the Saskatchewan situation and this particular case. Of 505 units allocated to Saskatchewan this year, none has been started as of yet. The reason is that circular "J-l" was introduced and is being very strictly enforced, at least to this point in time. I would like to ask the minister, to have the "J-l" circular withdrawn, or at least have the rules relaxed, so that many bands-some of the bands, or all of them-can meet the criteria that will allow them to begin their housing projects now. It is very unpleasant for anyone with experience in trying to build a house during the winter months, to meet the very stringent budget the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development sets for the Indian bands.
I would like to point out in respect of the school situation for the Buffalo River Band, that the province of Saskatchewan set up the Department of Northern Saskatchewan a number of years ago, in the early 1970s. As a result, communities of similar size and structure, not on reservation land, were built to great standards by the Department of Northern Saskatchewan. They have never at any time had better educational

June 29, 1982
Adjournment Debate
facilities. They have sewer and water in almost all of their housing projects. They are modern communities in which people are very proud to live.
That is not so on Indian reserves in northern Saskatchewan, in particular, and in the entire province in general, and we would like to see the standards of reserves raised significantly above what they have been to this point. It seems that the department is getting more and more heavily structured and leaning away from allowing Indian people to control their own destiny. It seems they have become dependent on the federal government and dependent upon a welfare handout sytem. They have little hope of building their economies or the economic bases on reserves so that they can seek some kind of self determination and be responsible for their own affairs. I believe the present ratio is about 33 to one; there is one federal government employee for every 33 treaty Indians in Canada. That number is growing all the time. We must start moving away from that and begin putting more control of what happens to treaty Indian people on their lands into their own hands.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-DELAY IN ON-RESERVE HOUSING PROGRAM. (B) CONSTRUCTION OF SCHOOL AT DILLON, SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chenier), let me say that I will not have time in the three minutes allotted to me to respond to all the hon. member's concerns, but I will address his last concern first, that is, his concern about "J" circulars.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) has been asked to suspend his department's "J" circulars which relate to the Indian on-reserve housing program. The reason given for this request is to allow the housing
program on Indian reserves in Saskatchewan to begin. First let me say there is nothing in the "J" circulars themselves which prevents the housing program from beginning in Saskatchewan or, for that matter, in any other region of this department.
Until very recently, the departmental guidelines concerning the Indian on-reserve housing program were contained in the department's circular No. 57. That circular has been updated and included in a series of departmental circulars with alphabetical designations. The designation for community services and housing is "J". This circular reflects the government's concern about Indian on-reserve housing and that the performance of the housing program on Indian reserves meets its targets.
In these circulars Indian bands are asked to identify all the funding sources to complete a housing project before appropriated capital is released to the band. This will avoid the situation where housing projects end up underfunded, resulting in incompleted houses. This identification of sources has been a requirement of the program for some time. This position was discussed with Indian leaders from Saskatchewan during the week of June 14. Meetings are being held now, and will continue in the near future, to familiarize departmental staff and Indian bands with these new program guidelines.
I recommend that the hon. member write directly to the minister about the particular band he was discussing tonight.
